newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Soycomplex surge puts Europe's buyers on back foot.
newsitem.headline: Soycomplex surge puts Europe's buyers on back foot.

text.p: Another strong surge in the Chicago soybean complex on Friday is expected to add to the woes of European feeds consumers this week, with most still limited to buying cover for only immediate needs.

A combination of a fund-driven, soaring futures market in the United States and a firm dollar have left feed customers in Europe, who have to buy some supplies, paying the highest prices for material in years.
"People are having to cover in soymeal for the next few months, There are no complete replacements for this," commented Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.
In the near term, a dollar slipping off its highs may prompt some to come to the market today and take cover but traders noted in historical terms prices were still prohibitively high.
The dollar was trading around 1.8980 against the guilder on Monday morning against 1.9230 on Friday.

Traders said the feed combination of soymeal and tapioca was continuing to lose out to much cheaper feed grains. They said feed grains were trading at around 32.50 guilders per 100 kg against 60 guilders for soymeal and around 20 for tapioca.

But another factor is the onset of spring in the northern hemisphere, when cattle are taken out into the fields to graze, denting general demand for feeds. "This will mean compounders may not be so swift in coming to the market," one said.

According to Van Dijk's calculations, the physical market for soymeal in Europe is likely to remain tight for the next few months. Based on arrivals, he sees the first ample supplies of soymeal from Brazil hitting European shores in June.
"Until then the situation will remain tight," he said.

In addition there are fears Brazil could impose a three percent tax on its soybean exports, the main factor behind the latest fund buying spree in Chicago. Brazilian crushers, whose profits have been squeezed since the abolition of the tax last year, would benefit from the discouragement to exports and consequently cheaper domestic supplies.
Traders here were still sceptical, saying that if the rumour proved to be false, the market could correct sharply downwards.
"But really, it's in the hands of the funds," one said.
Flows of speculative money in the United States were also behind Van Dijk predicting that despite the tight physical situation, prices could ease a little in April.
"I think we'll see the top of the market this month -- the funds aren't looking to Europe (where the market is tight) and we could see them liquidating beans and meal," he said.
Elsewhere, traders were citing reports of lower forecasts for the Argentine sunseed crop, expected in a few months time. Brokers said this could underpin prices this week.
